solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Group backing US city’s electric car

indicators.note: to back is to move backwards, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a set is a group of things that go together
LA is Los Angeles

explanation.surface: A group of backers in an American city is funding an electric car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' reads as financial support, but it tells you to turn the group round.
explanation.definitionFit: Tesla is the maker of a well-known range of battery-powered vehicles, so its name stands for one of its models.

clue.text: Grass up gutless editor, a drunkard

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, the wrong way round
without guts means with the insides removed, leaving only the outside pair

blocks.note: grass and pot are both slang for cannabis
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone informs on a cowardly editor who drinks too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass up' looks like the British slang for informing on someone; here grass is the drug, and up turns it over. TOP + ER gives TOPER.
explanation.definitionFit: A toper is an old-fashioned word for a heavy habitual drinker, the same meaning as drunkard.

clue.text: Clicks on recent photograph

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing sitting on another is placed above it, so it comes first

blocks.note: snaps are sharp clicking sounds, as of fingers
hot news is fresh and recent

explanation.surface: Someone taps on the latest picture on a phone screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clicks on' sounds like tapping a link, but it is one piece placed on top of another.
explanation.definitionFit: A snapshot is an informal, quickly taken photo, so it is a kind of photograph.

clue.text: A Mafia boss is a handsome chap

blocks.note: taken as written
the title given to the head of a Mafia family
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gangster chief turns out to be very good-looking.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a plain statement, but every word before the definition is a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Adonis was the beautiful youth loved by Aphrodite in Greek myth, and the name is used for any strikingly attractive young man.

clue.text: What might persuade a couple of Romeos into bed?

indicators.note: to go into something is to end up inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
Romeo is R in the NATO alphabet, and a couple means two of them
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: What could tempt a pair of lovers into bed together?
explanation.walkthrough: Romeos look like lovers, but Romeo is the radio code word for R. The definition is a whole question, since a reward can coax anyone, not only lovers.
explanation.definitionFit: A carrot is an incentive dangled to coax someone, from the idea of a carrot held before a donkey.

clue.text: Island broadcaster’s announcement

indicators.note: an announcement is spoken out, so we go by the sound rather than the spelling

blocks.note: Sky is a British satellite TV company

explanation.surface: A TV channel makes an announcement about an island.
explanation.walkthrough: Sky is a major British television broadcaster; its name is pronounced exactly like the island.
explanation.definitionFit: Skye is the largest island of the Inner Hebrides, off the west coast of Scotland.

clue.text: Nice to get rid of large worker on the land

indicators.note: getting rid of something removes it, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: nice and pleasant are synonyms
L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing sizes

explanation.surface: A French city wants to be rid of a big farm labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice at the start of the clue hides its lower-case sense behind the capital: it is the adjective, not the French city.
explanation.definitionFit: A peasant is a small farmer or agricultural labourer, someone who works the soil.

clue.text: Doctor not masked? I’ve no idea

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with or alter, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Is the doctor unmasked? Someone shrugs that they have no idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a person, but it is a verb meaning to alter.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are idiomatic replies meaning the speaker does not know the answer to a question.

clue.text: Ancient relative’s northeastern heartland destroyed

indicators.note: something destroyed is wrecked, so its letters are broken up and rebuilt

blocks.note: NE is the abbreviation for northeastern
taken as written

explanation.surface: An old family member's home region in the northeast has been ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relative' suggests a grandparent, but the relative is a cousin species of modern humans.
explanation.definitionFit: Neanderthals were an extinct prehistoric human species closely related to our own, so they are an ancient kin of ours.

clue.text: Philosopher quietly left at end of concerto

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: p (piano) is the musical direction for quietly
L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A thinker slipped out silently as the concerto finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quietly' is P from musical notation, where p (piano) tells the player to play softly.
explanation.definitionFit: Plato was the ancient Greek thinker, student of Socrates, who founded the Academy in Athens.

clue.text: Bald Cockney is so stuffy

indicators.note: a London Cockney accent famously drops the aitch at the start of words

blocks.note: bald means without hair on the head

explanation.surface: A bald Londoner complains that it is very stuffy.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney is a working-class East Londoner, whose accent drops the H at the start of words, so HAIRLESS loses its H.
explanation.definitionFit: A stuffy room lacks fresh ventilation, which is what airless describes.

clue.text: Stormy rains engulfing America from land west of Alaska

indicators.note: stormy weather is turbulent, so the letters are tossed into a new order
to engulf is to swallow up, so one piece ends up surrounded by another

blocks.note: taken as written
US is the United States

explanation.surface: Heavy storms sweep over America, blowing in from across the Bering Strait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stormy rains' reads as weather, but stormy only tells you to mix the letters of the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Russia lies just across the Bering Strait from Alaska, so its adjective describes something coming from there.

clue.text: Loves anecdotes one collects

indicators.note: a collection gathers things inside it, so the letters are held within the words

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone adores stories that a friend has gathered.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from the middle of the first word into the start of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To dote on someone is to be excessively fond of them, a verb phrase matching loves.

clue.text: Boat sure to be wrecked — by me?

definitions.text: Boat sure to be wrecked — by me?

indicators.note: a wreck is something smashed apart, so the letters are broken and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone muses on who might be responsible for wrecking a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: the person who wrecks the boat is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A saboteur deliberately damages or destroys property, so wrecking a vessel is exactly their work.

clue.text: Summary going over everyone’s head? That’s correct

indicators.note: in a down clue, going over something means sitting above it, so it comes first
the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a précis is a short summary of a text
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A summary goes over everyone's heads, and someone agrees that is right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going over everyone's head' suggests being too hard to understand; here it just places one piece above a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Precise means exact or accurate, the same sense as correct when describing a figure or statement.

clue.text: Increasingly irritated with scruffy attire, right?

indicators.note: scruffy means untidy and messed up, so the letters are put in disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone is getting more and more annoyed about shabby clothes, aren't they?
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of ATTIRE is followed by R.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratty is informal British slang for bad-tempered, so its comparative form means more annoyed than before.

clue.text: Keen camper sleeping here

blocks.note: first meaning: eager and determined
second meaning, split into two words: where a camper spends the night

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic camper is asleep at this spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning reads as two words, IN TENT, the place a camper sleeps.
explanation.definitionFit: Being intent on something means being eager and determined about it, so the adjective matches keen.

clue.text: Go AWOL in the Sahara perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: to leave the army without permission
second meaning: an example of a vast arid region

explanation.surface: A soldier runs off without leave somewhere in North Africa's sands.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb and the noun are spelt the same but stressed differently.
explanation.definitionFit: AWOL means absent without leave, and a soldier who abandons their post deserts; the Sahara is the largest hot arid region on Earth.

clue.text: Helpful purchase for the climber?

blocks.note: surface reading: a useful bit of kit bought in an outdoor shop
setter's reading: purchase means grip, a small ledge where a climber can wedge a foot

explanation.surface: Someone recommends a handy thing to buy for a mountaineer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Purchase' suggests shopping, but it also means a firm grip or foothold.
explanation.definitionFit: A toehold is a small hold for the toes on a rock face, giving a climber just enough grip.

clue.text: Old-fashioned duke had died

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for duke
to have a meal is to eat it
d. is the abbreviation for died, as in family trees

explanation.surface: A fusty old aristocrat had passed away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had' reads as an auxiliary verb, but it is the past of having dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dated has gone out of fashion and belongs to an earlier period.

clue.text: Sounds like con man spotted cat

indicators.note: what something sounds like is how it is said, not how it is written

blocks.note: a con man cheats people; in a non-rhotic British accent the final R is silent

explanation.surface: Someone says a swindler has been seen near a wild cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' looks like seen, but it describes the cat's coat. The homophone relies on British speech, where the final R of cheater is not pronounced.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheetah is a big African feline with a coat covered in black spots.

clue.text: Nobleman in good time? Not quite

indicators.note: not quite complete means falling short, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: to be in good time is to be early

explanation.surface: Has a lord arrived punctually? Not quite.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for arriving ahead of time loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An earl is a British peer ranking above a viscount and below a marquess.

clue.text: Still time for meeting

blocks.note: still and even both intensify a comparison: still better, even better
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: There is still time to get to the meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like the everyday adverb about time remaining, but here it is the intensifier.
explanation.definitionFit: A meeting such as a race meeting is an organised occasion or sporting fixture, which is one sense of event.

clue.text: Unknown person going round lake, a killer perhaps

indicators.note: going round something means encircling it, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a stranger is someone you do not know
L is the abbreviation for lake on maps

explanation.surface: A mysterious figure walking round a lake turns out to be a murderer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks the definition as an example: this is one kind of killer.
explanation.definitionFit: A strangler murders by throttling, so such a person is one type of murderer.

clue.text: Ready to drop, tried pushing Republican back

indicators.note: pushing something out of place moves it from where it was
putting something back further along means reinserting it later in the word

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: An exhausted campaigner tried shoving a Republican out of the way.
explanation.walkthrough: The R in TRIED moves one place further back, giving TIRED.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready to drop is an idiom for being so exhausted you could collapse, which describes someone tired.
